transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-03-11 16:00 UTC | Duration: 63 min | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramos (Redwood SE), David Kim (Lynx - Infra), Priya Shah (Lynx - ML Infra), Elena Torres (Lynx - Security), Marcus Li (Lynx - Ops)

Summary (auto): quick deep dive on air-gapped artifact delivery, kernel module provisioning for NVIDIA drivers, offline license activation flow, and runtime tuning (KV cache/batching/quantiz). Agreed to exchange manifest template and schedule on-prem window.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Morgan: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'll hand it to sofia and then we'll go through the end-to-end — artifact arrival, driver + module, and the redwood runtime tuning notes.
[00:00:22] David: awesome, thx. quick context, we're doing the sealed deployment in our colo cages, it's fully air-gapped, courier arrives next tuesday with drives. main goal is predictable 95p latency under 1.2s for 512-token inference, throughput around 300 tokens/s per node.
[00:00:40] Sofia: got it. can you confirm the machines? gpu models, kernel versions, and if secure boot is enabled? those change kernel module install steps.
[00:00:51] David: rack is 4 x A100 80GB per host, RHEL 8.8, kernel 5.14, secure boot currently enabled but we can toggle during proc if needed.
[00:01:05] Sofia: okay A100s — main differences we'll highlight: nvidia-driver 525 vs 535 vs 540, cuda 11.8 vs 12.1. for our runtime we recommend 535+ but we have a 525 compatibility matrix as well. we'll send a short doc.
[00:01:24] Priya: question — for air-gapped installs do you expect us to build DKMS or do you provide prebuilt signed modules? secure boot and module signing is a blocker for us.
[00:01:36] Morgan: good call out. we provide signed kernel modules for supported kernels and an install script that loads them with MOK enrolment steps. for fully locked-down envs we also support a DKMS build flow; note that requires compilers on the target and increases install time.
[00:01:54] Elena: module signing — do you sign with your key? how does that interact with our secure boot policy and our internal key management?
[00:02:04] Sofia: we ship modules signed with our build key. typical pattern we recommend: you either add our public MOK to your allowed key list during install window, or we provide unsigned modules plus build instructions so your security team can sign with your internal key. both options documented.
[00:02:22] Marcus: logistics — for the artifact transfer we're using encrypted HDDs with LUKS, courier chain-of-custody, and a signed manifest. how do we validate integrity on your side?
[00:02:34] Morgan: sha256 + GPG-signed manifest. we'll provide a sample manifest and verification steps. also include the encrypted container hash so you can verify at reception before we decrypt.
[00:02:50] David: will there be a license file that needs to be activated online? we are air-gapped so online calls are no-go.
[00:02:58] Sofia: we support offline license activation. process: you place the .lic in the sealed media, on install you generate a hardware nonce (HSM-tied or host fingerprint), we return an activation blob that you import. for extra security you can bind license to TPM/SGX/HSM — we have options.
[00:03:16] Elena: what about rotation and emergency revocation? if keys are compromised how fast can we revoke?
[00:03:23] Morgan: we have a short grace period (configurable) and an emergency revocation manifest we can ship; for air-gapped setups revocation happens at the next maintenance window unless you have an internal policy to enforce earlier. we discussed out-of-band signed revocation lists in previous calls.
[00:03:36] Priya: shifting gears — runtime perf: we care about cold-start vs warmed KV cache. how much improvement are we typically seeing when KV is pre-warmed?
[00:03:46] Sofia: depends on sequence distribution and prefix reuse. for chat-like workloads with long prefixes and high reuse we see 2-5x reduction in tail latency after pre-warm. if your workload is stateless bursts, benefits drop. we recommend a KV replay script that hits the model with representative prompts during maintenance to populate cache.
[00:04:06] David: is that script safe to run in production? it will add load.
[00:04:10] Sofia: yes, do it on a canary subset or during low-traffic windows; also our runtime supports background low-priority pre-warm jobs pinned to spare GPU cycles.
[00:04:22] Marcus: for disk layout — we want KV cache on NVMe or in memory? what's your standard?
[00:04:28] Sofia: best is NVMe-backed mmap with HugePages for pinned memory fragments. we also support a hybrid: hot KV in GPU memory (when enough VRAM) and cold KV on NVMe. put model weights on NVMe and enable direct NVMe->GPU DMA if kernel supports it.
[00:04:45] Priya: GPU memory is tight on A100 80GB with larger context windows; any tips to tune batch size to hit throughput without blowing latency?
[00:04:53] Sofia: yes — start with batch size 1 for latency SLOs, use continuous batching (our runtime packs requests for compatible seq lengths) and set a batching window (20-50ms). then increase concurrency slots until you hit the 95p target. we'll share a tuning spreadsheet that maps sequence length distribution to recommended batch windows.
[00:05:10] David: quantization — we want to move to 4-bit for cost, but worried about hallucinations. what's your experience?
[00:05:16] Sofia: quantization gains are workload dependent. 4-bit (GPTQ-style) often yields 2-4x memory reduction with minimal quality loss on instruction tasks, but for sensitive generative tasks we suggest A/B evals. we also support per-layer mixed-quant profiles and recommend keeping first/last layers higher precision. we'll include quant profile examples and eval harness.
[00:05:35] Priya: do you recommend int8 dynamic for throughput?
[00:05:38] Sofia: int8 dynamic can help on some ops but depends on kernel support. our runtime can fallback to fp16 kernels if int8 path isn't available; there is a throughput/accuracy tradeoff.
[00:05:49] Morgan: small note — some customers saw regressions when switching quant profiles without rerunning their prompt evals; track a baseline.
[00:05:56] Elena: security — how do you handle model artifacts that might contain PII? storage encryption at rest on NVMe? audit logs?
[00:06:04] Sofia: we encrypt artifacts at rest with customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). audit logs are provided in the private install package (local console), and we support token-scoped access control and RBAC.
[00:06:15] David: kernel tuning: any recommended sysctl for NUMA and CPU isolation for the inference threads?
[00:06:21] Sofia: pin inference threads with numactl to the CPU sockets local to GPUs, disable CPU frequency scaling for predictable latency, set vm.nr_hugepages large enough for model mappings, and disable transparent hugepages (THP) on RHEL for stability. also tune IO scheduler to noop for NVMe.
[00:06:41] Marcus: NCCL / interconnect — cross-host performance is important for multi-GPU models. we're using RoCE over our fabric. any special config?
[00:06:48] Sofia: for RoCE set proper MTU, enable dcqcn, and ensure PFC is configured. we recommend NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME setting to pick the fabric interface and tuning NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING for resiliency. for air-gapped stacks ensure you have the right firmware versions for the NIC to match RoCE requirements.
[00:07:06] Priya: a nit — you mentioned direct NVMe->GPU DMA, is that via GPUDirect Storage? what kernel/CUDA combos required?
[00:07:12] Sofia: GPUDirect Storage requires recent drivers — generally CUDA 11.8+ and driver 525+ plus kernel support. we'll provide an exact matrix based on your kernel. if GPUDirect isn't available we fall back to host-scatter which is slightly slower.
[00:07:28] David: on the manifest and signed artifacts — will you include checksums for each model shard and the runtime binary?
[00:07:34] Morgan: yes. manifest lists model shards, runtime tarball, kernel modules, license blob, and a per-file sha256. it's GPG-signed. we also include a JSON map for compatibility but in air-gapped mode we provide a human-readable manifest too.
[00:07:47] Elena: what about time sync? license nonces rely on clock. do you require NTP to external servers?
[00:07:53] Sofia: we do require accurate time for certificate validation. for air-gapped set-ups customers run a local NTP server inside the VPC or use a hardware time source. we support an offline validation window to tolerate small skews, but long-term you need reliable time.
[00:08:07] Marcus: during install, what's the rollback story if a driver push causes nodes to fail?
[00:08:12] Sofia: installer creates a snapshot of the previous driver state and leaves an automated rollback hook. for critical environments we recommend a staged rollout: canary host -> small pool -> full fleet. the installer logs everything to the offbox audit file for troubleshooting.
[00:08:25] David: performance targets — if we see >1.2s 95p at 512 tokens after tuning, what's the escalation path?
[00:08:31] Morgan: open a support ticket with perf traces. our SEs will run a guided perf session, we may ask for a small benchmark harness and reproduce in our testbed if needed. we can propose changes: kernel tweaks, batch window adjustments, or alternative quant profiles.
[00:08:44] Priya: tracer and logs — what traces do you need? metrics exported?
[00:08:48] Sofia: we ingest per-token latency traces, GPU util, mem usage, KV hit/miss rates, and batching telemetry. the private console ships a prometheus exporter and a trace collector. we also provide a minimal trace uploader for offline sharing (encrypted).
[00:09:02] Marcus: one operational question — if we need a hotfix for a module, can you ship a signed patch that we install offline?
[00:09:08] Morgan: yes — we have a signed hotfix channel and an emergency signing workflow. we'll want to validate on one host first.
[00:09:15] David: ok great. can we do a dry-run of the install but without production keys so we validate steps?
[00:09:20] Sofia: absolutely — we provide a sandbox manifest and dummy license file for validation. use the sandbox key to enrol MOK and test DKMS builds.
[00:09:29] Priya: quick perf number question — what's a realistic tokens/s for a single A100 at 80GB for a 70b model with fp16 vs 4-bit?
[00:09:36] Sofia: approximate: fp16 you might get around 500-700 tokens/s depending on prompt shapes and batching; with 4-bit quant you can see 900-1,200 tokens/s, but again depends on sequence lengths and kernel availability. these are ballpark, we'll provide numbers from our benchmark harness.
[00:09:52] Elena: are there any legal / export constraints on shipping model artifacts? we need to confirm with procurement.
[00:09:58] Morgan: yes please check — some models have licensing restrictions around offline distribution. we'll include license summaries in the manifest and flag any restricted models.
[00:10:08] David: can we get a checklist for the courier arrival? what checks should ops do before powering on hosts?
[00:10:13] Morgan: yes — checklist includes verifying seals, verifying sha256 of encrypted container, verifying courier signature, powering on one host in maintenance network, verifying MOK enrolment flow, and only then decrypt artifacts. we'll share a single-page checklist.
[00:10:26] Marcus: and physical chain-of-custody — we'll attach CCTV and sign-off forms.
[00:10:30] Morgan: perfect. we'll add that to the manifest guidance.
[00:10:34] Sofia: one more runtime note — if you're using long context windows: KV cache size scales with context length, consider two knobs: kv eviction policy (LRU vs TTL) and partitioning frequently-accessed prefixes into a hot-shard pinned in GPU VRAM.
[00:10:50] Priya: is there tooling to observe KV hit/miss at per-route level?
[00:10:54] Sofia: yes our console telemetry shows per-route KV hit rates and per-token cost. for private installs we ship the same dashboard with local retention.
[00:11:03] David: good. final — what's the expected timeline from courier arrival to full production?
[00:11:09] Morgan: typical: Day 0 courier arrival + integrity checks; Day 1 install + driver/module + license import; Day 2 perf tuning + KV pre-warm + smoke tests; Day 3 canary traffic. total ~3-5 days depending on ops bandwidth.
[00:11:23] Elena: ok that's acceptable.
[00:11:25] Morgan: recap and next steps: we'll send signed manifest template, driver compatibility matrix, install checklist, and sandbox manifest + dummy license. schedule the install window — david to propose times.
[00:11:36] David: i'll ping ops and propose next wed/thurs for the courier — will update by friday.
[00:11:41] Morgan: great. any last q's?
[00:11:43] Priya: just one — could you share the perf harness and example prompts?
[00:11:46] Sofia: yes we'll add that to the shared folder along with quant-profiles.
[00:11:50] Morgan: thanks all, logging action items now. meeting end.
